description:
Hey everyone! We are AeroZone. We bring solid knowledge and experience in solving GN&C problems for UAVs, and we’re jumping into the next NASA Space Apps Challenge!

We’re looking for passionate teammates to join us. If you’ve got strong skills in C++, Python, Vibe Coding, AI/Machine Learning, or Data Processing, we’d love to have you on board!
summary:
MARS ODYSSEY is a tablet mission planner, shown as a web app for this demo, for the first crewed walks on Mars. It’s set in Jezero Crater, where Perseverance is exploring today.

It’s built on real NASA data: HiRISE elevation models, orbital imagery, Perseverance’s actual traverse, its sample sites and its weather records. We turned the terrain into slope, roughness and hazard maps. Pick a start and a destination, and the planner offers three routes, from direct to cautious, and explains the trade-offs. Then watch a rover or astronaut drive the route in a physics-based 3D simulation, steering around boulders and craters with a simulated lidar sensor. Today these are simulations, but the same navigation could one day guide a real rover.

A “world” mode puts several rovers and astronauts on the map at once, each with a battery or oxygen supply that runs down over time. When an astronaut’s oxygen drops too low, the app raises an alert and suggests the nearest rover to send. It simulates a real working environment, where cooperation is vital.

Why it matters: on Mars, help is twenty light-minutes away. Crews will have to plan routes, manage their consumables and coordinate rescues on their own. MARS ODYSSEY lets people practise those decisions on real Martian terrain before anyone lands, and could later help astronauts navigate and work together on Mars.
details:
What it does and how it works

MARS ODYSSEY is a mission planner for the first crewed walks on Mars. It’s designed for a tablet carried by the crew or the habitat team, and shown here as a web app. Everything takes place in Jezero Crater, the area Perseverance is exploring now, so the terrain, sample sites and weather are real.

The app has four connected parts:

1. The map and data layers. We processed NASA’s HiRISE elevation model of Jezero into slope, roughness and hazard maps at 5-metre resolution. These sit on top of orbital imagery from NASA Mars Trek (CTX and HiRISE), together with:

  • Perseverance’s real traverse;
  • the sites where it sealed rock samples;
  • weather recorded by its MEDA instrument, sol by sol;
  • space-weather and radiation information on a Safety tab.

Users can also mark their own locations with their own icons: HQ, geological sites, cargo, supplies, greenhouses and danger points. Each can have notes attached.

2. The route planner. Pick a start and a destination, and the planner searches the hazard map for three alternative routes: direct, balanced and cautious. Each comes with its distance, slope, hazard exposure, climb and an estimated walking time. A short explanation says why one is recommended, and an elevation profile shows what the walk will feel like.

3. The 3D simulation. Any route can be driven in a 3D model of the crater, either by Perseverance or by a suited astronaut.

  • The rover runs in a real physics engine under Mars gravity (3.711 m/s²). The astronaut follows the terrain at a walking pace that slows on slopes.
  • After you leave the 3D view, the simulation keeps running behind the map, so the plan and the “live” situation sit on one screen.

4. Obstacle avoidance: lidar and depth sensing. The route planner only knows what orbit can see, at 5 m resolution, so a boulder or small crater inside one map cell is invisible to it. The vehicle has to find those hazards itself. We gave it a simulated lidar, a laser scanner like the ones on self-driving cars, and use its data in two complementary ways.

  • The scan: the sensor sits 2 m up and sweeps all the way round in 1.5° steps, from 45° below the horizon to 15° above it, out to 10 m. It takes about five scans per simulated second, plus a new one every half-metre of travel. It measures the real 3D shapes of the boulders and the carved terrain.
  • Boulders, from the point cloud plus the depth image: a boulder is a positive obstacle, something sticking up. The point cloud (a top-down map of every laser hit) shows where it is and how big. The depth image (a colour-coded picture: near is red, far is blue) shows it as a sudden “near” patch standing out from the ground behind it. Any return more than 30 cm above the orbital ground model is marked as an obstacle.
  • Craters, from the depth image: a crater is a negative obstacle, a hole, which is much harder to see. A laser doesn’t hit the inside of a hole; the ground simply “falls away”. The depth image reveals that: where the terrain should continue, the measured distance jumps further away or disappears. Anything more than 30 cm below the expected surface, and any shadowed area the laser can’t see behind a rim, is marked as dangerous.
    • If the way is blocked, the vehicle backs up and tries again.
    • Its state is always shown: on route, detouring, backing up or blocked.
    • Once the route ahead is clear, it rejoins it.
  • Consistent world: craters are carved directly into the terrain model. The physics engine, the 3D graphics and the lidar therefore all see the same ground. There is no case where the screen shows a crater the sensor can’t detect.

Both the point cloud and the depth image are shown live on screen, so you can watch the vehicle “see” the obstacle and swerve.

World demo. Several rovers and astronauts share the crater at once.

  • They wander, travel to locations, or intercept each other. Interception aims at where a moving target will be, not where it is.
  • Each carries a battery or an oxygen supply that runs down over time.
  • When an astronaut’s oxygen falls below 30 %, an alert appears. One tap shows the closest rover with an estimated arrival time, and a second sends it.
  • You can ride along with any object, drive it with the keyboard or an on-screen joystick, or hand it back to autonomy.
  • On-ground arrows point to the nearest location and colleague of each type.

An AI assistant, the Odyssey Copilot, answers questions in plain language (“what was the weather on sol 300?”, “plan a route to Cheyava Falls”) and drives the map for you.

Benefits

  • Safer decisions: risk is visible before anyone leaves the habitat, as hazard, slope and distance side by side rather than one “shortest” line.
  • Two layers of safety: orbital data plans the route, and on-board sensing catches what orbit misses.
  • Rehearsal: crews can practise traverses and emergencies on real terrain, as often as they like, at no cost.
  • Shared awareness: everyone, everything and every important place appears on one map with live status.
  • Accessible: it runs in a browser, so students and the public can explore the real Jezero Crater too.

Intended impact

On Mars, help is up to twenty light-minutes away. Crews will plan their own routes, ration their consumables and organise rescues with little help from Earth. We want MARS ODYSSEY to be the place where those skills are practised before launch, and a starting point for a real field tool. The navigation and obstacle-avoidance logic in the simulation could one day guide an actual rover. In the classroom, it turns NASA’s open data into something people can walk through.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript and Python, plus a little HTML/CSS.
  • Front end: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet (maps), Recharts (charts), Three.js (3D view).
  • Simulation: Python with aiohttp (WebSockets), PyBullet physics, and a pure-pursuit path follower.
  • Obstacle avoidance: a custom virtual lidar, NumPy ray casting against the terrain and boulder shapes. It produces a point cloud and a depth image, feeding a positive/negative obstacle classifier, a local hazard grid, and an arc-based planner with recovery behaviour. Scans are streamed to the browser in a compact binary format.
  • Route planner: FastAPI with a hazard-weighted A* search over the terrain grid.
  • Data pipeline: GDAL, Rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, GeoPandas, Shapely, PyProj.
  • Data: HiRISE elevation model (USGS/NASA), NASA Mars Trek imagery, the JPL rover traverse and sample records, MEDA weather, space-weather feeds, NASA’s 3D Perseverance model.
  • AI: Llama 3.3 70B through OpenRouter, with an offline fallback so the app still answers without internet.
  • Engineering: pixi pins every package version, so the whole team runs an identical environment on Windows, macOS and Linux. Git and GitHub with a shared integration branch. Automated tests for the physics, navigation, obstacle avoidance and server.
  • Hardware: ordinary laptops; nothing specialised is needed to run it.

What makes it creative

  • Map and simulation are one system: the planner and the 3D world are joined. You plan on the map, step into the 3D view, step back out, and the map keeps showing the objects living their lives.
  • Seeing holes, not just rocks: most simple obstacle avoiders only detect things that stick up. Using the depth image to spot ground that “falls away” lets ours avoid craters too, the hazard that is easiest to miss and most dangerous to fall into.
  • Two kinds of sensing: the orbital map plans the big picture, and the vehicle’s own sensor handles what orbit can’t resolve. This mirrors how Perseverance drives itself (AutoNav).
  • Interception, not chasing: rescue rovers aim for where a moving astronaut will be, and slow down for rough ground.
  • Consumables drive the story: battery and oxygen turn route planning into resource management and teamwork.
  • Real place: this is real Mars terrain and real rover history, not a made-up landscape.

What our team considered

  • Accuracy vs. speed: real elevation data at 5 m resolution, true Mars gravity, and a full lidar scan, while staying smooth in a browser. Distant objects are drawn as simple squares; only nearby ones get full 3D models.
    • the hazard map is labelled as a model, not a guarantee;
    • arrival times say they are straight-line estimates;
    • demo speeds are clearly marked as faster than the real rover.
  • Usability on a tablet: large touch targets, a virtual joystick, collapsible panels and a fixed legend.
  • Robustness: identical environments on every computer, automatic recovery if the physics fails, offline fallbacks for the AI and imagery.
  • Teamwork: the project is split into five modules owned by different people (data, route planning, interface, simulation, obstacle avoidance), joined through agreed interfaces and tested on a shared integration branch before release.
